passage: With film, every press of the shutter used up a frame that cost money to buy and develop, so a photographer had to decide in advance whether a moment was worth keeping. Digital cameras removed that cost, and photographers now routinely take dozens of nearly identical shots of a single scene. The decision did not disappear, one photography instructor argues; it simply moved. Much of a digital photographer's judgment is now exercised after the shoot, in ______ the many frames.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The decision that film forced before each shot, whether a moment was worth keeping, has moved to after the shoot, where the photographer must choose among dozens of near-identical frames, so the judgment lies in "culling" them. "Collating" the frames would gather and order them but would keep every one, and "cropping" and "captioning" improve or label a single frame; none of them is the decision about which moments to keep that the instructor says has moved.
